click-country.lead: Learn the {group} map by clicking each {unitName} when its name appears.
click-country.heading: How the click map quiz works
click-country.howToPlay: A {unitName} name appears above the map. Click it and keep going until the set is finished. The borders stay on the map, which makes this the easiest map mode to learn from.
click-country.tip: If one answer keeps getting you, remember one neighbor or coastline beside it. That is usually enough to find it next time.
click-country.skills: This is mostly about matching names to shapes and positions. After a while, the borders start looking familiar before you even read the whole prompt.
click-country.strategy: Look at the part of the map you are in and find one country you already know. The target is usually easier from there.
click-country.bestFor: For a map you barely know, this is usually the easiest place to start. It also works well as a refresher after leaving a region alone for a while.
click-country.mistakes: A familiar neighbor can look right for half a second. Check the border before clicking.

type-country.lead: Practice the names and locations of {groupTopic} by typing the highlighted {unitPlural}.
type-country.heading: How the typing map quiz works
type-country.howToPlay: One {unitName} is highlighted. Type its name and move on to the next one. You get the location as a clue, but the name has to come from memory.
type-country.tip: If you recognize the shape but the name is slow, say the name out loud or in your head before typing.
type-country.skills: You can know exactly where a place is and still blank on its name. This mode catches that gap fast.
type-country.strategy: Work out the region first. Nearby countries will often jog the name better than staring at the outline.
type-country.bestFor: Typing is useful once the shapes feel familiar but some of the names still lag behind.
type-country.mistakes: A similar shape can send you to the wrong name. Check where the highlight sits on the map.

find-country.lead: Test your knowledge of {groupTopic} by finding each {unitName} on a map with borders hidden.
find-country.heading: How the no-borders map quiz works
find-country.howToPlay: A {unitName} name appears on a map with the political borders hidden. Click where it belongs. The coastline stays, so you still have some geography to work with.
find-country.tip: Pick out a coastline, peninsula or big country you know and judge the target from there.
find-country.skills: Once the border lines disappear, you are relying on the layout in your head. Distance and neighbor order matter a lot more.
find-country.strategy: Ignore the whole map for a second. Find the right coast or subregion first and make the click from there.
find-country.bestFor: Borderless mode is a good follow-up once the normal click map has become comfortable.
find-country.mistakes: The empty interior makes people guess too early. There are still coastlines, corners and big shapes to use.

find-point.lead: Identify which {unitName} in this set contains each point placed on the map.
find-point.heading: How the point map quiz works
find-point.howToPlay: A point appears somewhere on the map. Type the {unitName} that actually contains it. The round keeps going through {countPhrase}.
find-point.tip: Points near borders are the nasty ones. Check which side of the border the dot is really on.
find-point.skills: This is good at exposing fuzzy boundaries. Knowing the general area is not much help when the point lands near an edge.
find-point.strategy: Notice whether the point is coastal, inland or on an island. That usually cuts the possibilities down quickly.
find-point.bestFor: Point mode works best on a map you already know pretty well. It exposes fuzzy boundaries quickly.
find-point.mistakes: A dot beside a famous country can still be across the border. Its exact side of the line decides the answer.

click-subdivision.lead: Learn {group} by clicking each {unitName} when its name appears.
click-subdivision.heading: How the subdivision click quiz works
click-subdivision.howToPlay: A {unitName} name appears. Click that subdivision on the map and continue through the set.
click-subdivision.tip: One familiar state or province nearby can make the rest of the area much easier.
click-subdivision.skills: You learn how the smaller pieces fit inside {groupTopic}, especially which ones touch and which shapes repeat.
click-subdivision.strategy: Find the part of {groupTopic} you are in. From there, use any subdivision you already know to narrow it down.
click-subdivision.bestFor: This is the easiest subdivision mode to begin with on a new map.
click-subdivision.mistakes: Two nearby subdivisions can look almost interchangeable. Compare the whole shape before clicking.

type-subdivision.heading: How the subdivision typing quiz works
type-subdivision.howToPlay: One {unitName} is highlighted. Type its name and continue through {countPhrase}.
type-subdivision.tip: Think about where the highlight sits inside the parent country. That often brings the name back.
type-subdivision.skills: Recognizing the right area is only half of it here. You also have to pull up the full subdivision name.
type-subdivision.strategy: Find the region inside {groupTopic} and think through the nearby subdivisions. The name usually comes faster with that context.
type-subdivision.bestFor: Typing is useful when the subdivision map looks familiar but the names are still slower than the shapes.
type-subdivision.mistakes: A partial name can feel convincing too early. Check the location before submitting it.

find-subdivision.lead: Test your knowledge of {groupTopic} by locating each {unitName} without subdivision borders.
find-subdivision.heading: How the no-borders subdivision quiz works
find-subdivision.howToPlay: The quiz names a {unitName} while the internal subdivision lines are hidden. Click where it belongs inside the parent country.
find-subdivision.tip: The outside shape of the country matters a lot here. Coasts and corners give you more than they seem to.
find-subdivision.skills: You have to remember the internal layout from memory once the subdivision lines are gone.
find-subdivision.strategy: Start with the edge of {groupTopic}. A coast, corner or big neighboring subdivision can give you a useful starting point.
find-subdivision.bestFor: This gets interesting once the bordered subdivision map has become comfortable.
find-subdivision.mistakes: The blank interior is still full of clues. The outside border, coast and corners can narrow the answer down a lot.

find-point-subdivision.lead: Identify which {unitName} in this set contains each point.
find-point-subdivision.heading: How the subdivision point quiz works
find-point-subdivision.howToPlay: A point appears inside one subdivision. Type the {unitName} that contains it.
find-point-subdivision.tip: Near a boundary, slow down and check which side the point is on.
find-point-subdivision.skills: This tests the parts of a subdivision far away from its best-known city or shape.
find-point-subdivision.strategy: Estimate where the point sits inside {groupTopic}. Its distance from the outer edge can be more useful than the nearest city.
find-point-subdivision.bestFor: This is mainly for subdivision maps whose basic outlines are already familiar.
find-point-subdivision.mistakes: A famous city nearby can pull you toward the wrong subdivision. The point itself decides the answer.
find-point-subdivision.displayName: Find the Subdivision from a Point

type-capital.lead: Practice the capitals of {groupTopic} while keeping each {unitName} tied to its place on the map.
type-capital.heading: How the capitals quiz works
type-capital.howToPlay: A {unitName} is highlighted and named. Type its capital. Smurdy marks the capital on the map for a moment before the next question.
type-capital.tip: Try to get the city from memory before you look for the answer dot.
type-capital.skills: The country and its capital stay tied to the same map, so you learn the city with some geographic context instead of as a loose flashcard fact.
type-capital.strategy: Picture the country first and say the capital before typing. The answer dot gives you a quick location check afterward.
type-capital.bestFor: Capital mode makes the most sense once the countries or states themselves are familiar.
type-capital.mistakes: The biggest city is not always the capital. A few countries are especially good at punishing that guess.

world.overview: World mixes every region into one round. A huge mainland country can be followed by a tiny island on the next question, so there is no single part of the map to settle into.
world.challenge: The hard part is the constant jump in scale. Europe can get crowded, and the Caribbean or Pacific can force a lot of zooming.
world.studyTip: World works best after the continent quizzes feel comfortable. It is good at exposing slow switches between regions.

us_states.overview: This set is the 50 US states. The western half gives you some big, obvious shapes; the Northeast and parts of the Midwest are much tighter.
us_states.challenge: The center and Northeast usually cause more misses because a lot of states are similar in size or packed together.
us_states.studyTip: Learn the states in chunks that make sense to you. The Great Lakes and Northeast are worth extra time if the middle keeps blending together.

europe.overview: Europe puts a lot of countries into a small map. The big peninsulas are easy to orient around, but the middle of the continent gets crowded fast.
europe.challenge: Central Europe and the Balkans are where a rough guess stops working. Several small countries sit only a short distance apart.
europe.studyTip: Know the big peninsulas and coastlines cold. Once those are automatic, the small-country clusters have somewhere to fit.

asia.overview: Asia is enormous, and the quiz can move from the Middle East to Central Asia or the Pacific coast in a few questions. Some regions have giant countries; others are packed tightly.
asia.challenge: Central Asia and mainland Southeast Asia are common trouble spots. The shapes are less forgiving when several neighbors sit close together.
asia.studyTip: Asia is easier to remember as several smaller maps. Central Asia and mainland Southeast Asia are the two parts most likely to deserve their own practice.

africa.overview: Africa has more than fifty answers in this set. The coast gives you a good outline, while the interior has long runs of neighboring countries that are harder to separate.
africa.challenge: West Africa gets crowded along the coast. Central and eastern Africa can be tough for the opposite reason: several large inland countries sit next to each other.
africa.studyTip: The coast gives the continent a useful skeleton. Once that is familiar, the landlocked countries have somewhere to sit.

south_america.overview: South America has only a dozen sovereign countries, so the whole set is manageable. Most of the trouble is near the north and around the two landlocked countries.
south_america.challenge: Guyana and Suriname are easy to swap. Bolivia and Paraguay also take longer if you only remember the coastline.
south_america.studyTip: Brazil is hard to miss and touches most of the continent. Use it as the country you check everything else against.

north_america.overview: This North America set includes the mainland, Central America and the sovereign Caribbean countries in Smurdy. Canada, the United States and Mexico take up most of the land area; the small-country work is farther south.
north_america.challenge: Central America is narrow, and the Caribbean puts a lot of small answers close together.
north_america.studyTip: The mainland is straightforward enough to learn first. Give the Caribbean its own practice until the islands stop blurring together.

middle_east.overview: This group covers the eastern Mediterranean, the Arabian Peninsula, Iran, Iraq and nearby western Asia. It is a much smaller set than all of Asia.
middle_east.challenge: The Gulf and the Levant have several small neighbors. A tiny shift on the map can put you in the wrong country.
middle_east.studyTip: Get the Arabian Peninsula fixed in your head. The smaller countries around it make more sense once that shape is familiar.

european_union.overview: This set is based on EU membership. Geography still matters, but the quiz also expects you to know which nearby European countries are outside the union.
european_union.challenge: A country can be surrounded by EU members and still not belong to the EU. That is where location knowledge alone stops helping.
european_union.studyTip: The shortest route is often learning the nearby non-members. Once those stand out, the membership map is easier to remember.

southeast_asia.overview: Southeast Asia has two very different-looking halves: the mainland around Thailand and Vietnam, and the island countries farther south and east.
southeast_asia.challenge: The mainland is tightly packed. Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines create a separate island problem.
southeast_asia.studyTip: Treat mainland and maritime Southeast Asia as two small maps until both feel easy.

latin_america.overview: Latin America stretches from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean into South America. It is a language-and-history grouping spread across a huge area.
latin_america.challenge: The quiz keeps changing map scale. An island question can be followed by a country covering a large part of South America.
latin_america.studyTip: South America and Central America are easier to learn on their own. Add the Caribbean after those two are solid.

spanish_speaking.overview: This set has the 20 sovereign countries where Spanish is an official or dominant national language. Most are in the Americas, with Spain and Equatorial Guinea far away from the rest.
spanish_speaking.challenge: The countries are spread across three continents. Nearby non-Spanish-speaking countries also make the set less obvious than a normal regional quiz.
spanish_speaking.studyTip: The American countries are the bulk of the set. Learn those by region, then remember the two outliers: Spain and Equatorial Guinea.

oceania.overview: Oceania gives you Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and the independent Pacific island countries. On the world map, many of the island answers are tiny and very far apart.
oceania.challenge: There are not many land borders to help you. A lot of the quiz comes down to remembering where each island group sits in the ocean.
oceania.studyTip: Know the big three first. The smaller islands are easier once you can place them relative to Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea.

central_america_and_caribbean.overview: This set combines the seven Central American mainland countries with the sovereign Caribbean islands. The two parts of the quiz feel quite different.
central_america_and_caribbean.challenge: Central America is a narrow chain. The Caribbean is mostly an island-order problem.
central_america_and_caribbean.studyTip: Learn Central America from Mexico down to Colombia. Practice the Caribbean separately until the island order starts to stick.
searchTerms: Central America and Caribbean map quiz
Caribbean and Central American countries quiz

caribbean_islands.overview: The Caribbean set focuses on the sovereign island countries in and around the Caribbean Sea. Cuba and Hispaniola are easy to see; many of the smaller islands are not.
caribbean_islands.challenge: Several answers are tiny at normal zoom, and some nearby islands are territories rather than sovereign-country answers.
caribbean_islands.studyTip: Start with the big islands you already recognize. The smaller eastern Caribbean countries are easier once you know where that chain begins and ends.

balkans.overview: The Balkans pack a lot of countries into southeastern Europe. The shapes are small enough that knowing the rough region is rarely enough.
balkans.challenge: The middle of the peninsula is full of short borders and similarly sized neighbors. Regional definitions also vary, so Smurdy uses one fixed country list.
balkans.studyTip: Learn who borders whom. For this region, neighbor order is more useful than memorizing each outline by itself.

eastern_europe.overview: Eastern Europe is a smaller slice of the Europe map using Smurdy's fixed group list. The exact definition changes from source to source, but the quiz list does not.
eastern_europe.challenge: A lot of the countries are inland or share long borders. They are easier to confuse when you rely on outline shape alone.
eastern_europe.studyTip: Poland, Ukraine and the Black Sea give you enough structure to place most of the rest.

mena.overview: MENA runs from Morocco across North Africa to the Middle East and Iran. It crosses two continents, which is part of why the full set feels bigger than the name suggests.
mena.challenge: North Africa is spread out; the eastern Mediterranean and Gulf are much tighter.
mena.studyTip: North Africa is basically a west-to-east chain. Learn that part first and the Middle East will feel like a separate, smaller problem.
searchTerms: Middle East and North Africa countries quiz

west_africa.overview: West Africa has a crowded Atlantic coast and a broad inland Sahel. Nigeria and Ghana are familiar to many players, but several smaller coastal countries sit right beside them.
west_africa.challenge: The coastline is where most close misses happen. Inland, the large shapes can also blend together.
west_africa.studyTip: The coast has a useful order. Once that order is familiar, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger are much easier to place behind it.

southern_europe.overview: Southern Europe is built around the Mediterranean-facing part of the continent: Iberia, Italy, Greece, nearby islands and the smaller states in the region.
southern_europe.challenge: The famous peninsulas are easy. The microstates and compact Balkan borders are where the precision starts.
southern_europe.studyTip: If Spain, Italy and Greece are automatic, the small countries around them are much easier to organize.

east_africa.overview: East Africa in Smurdy includes the Horn, the Great Lakes area, the Indian Ocean coast and nearby islands. The coast has several memorable shapes, while the inland countries are more compact.
east_africa.challenge: The Great Lakes area gets crowded quickly. Regional definitions also differ near central and southern Africa, so this quiz follows Smurdy's stored list.
east_africa.studyTip: The Horn and the Indian Ocean coast are the easiest places to recognize. Learn those well and work inland from them.

south_and_central_asia.overview: This group joins the Indian subcontinent with the landlocked countries north of it. India and Kazakhstan take up a lot of the map, with much smaller neighbors around them.
south_and_central_asia.challenge: Central Asian names are easy to mix up, and South Asia squeezes several countries into narrow spaces around India.
south_and_central_asia.studyTip: Think of this as two neighborhoods. India is the obvious center of one; Kazakhstan is the big one in the other.
searchTerms: South and Central Asia map quiz

northern_and_western_europe.overview: This group covers the British Isles, Scandinavia, the Nordic area and much of western continental Europe. Long coastlines give way to a much denser center.
northern_and_western_europe.challenge: Benelux and nearby small countries demand more precision than the big northern shapes.
northern_and_western_europe.studyTip: The North Sea is a useful center for this set. Once the countries around it are fixed, the rest spreads out pretty naturally.
searchTerms: Northern and Western Europe map quiz

central_and_southern_africa.overview: This set runs from the Congo Basin down to the southern end of Africa. It includes a mix of very large inland countries and several compact states around South Africa.
central_and_southern_africa.challenge: The two Congos are an obvious source of mistakes. Farther south, the countries get smaller and tighter together.
central_and_southern_africa.studyTip: Learn the Congo Basin and southern Africa as two separate patches before mixing the whole set.
searchTerms: Central and Southern Africa map quiz

sub_saharan_africa.overview: This is the large Africa set with North Africa removed. It still spans the west, center, east and south of the continent.
sub_saharan_africa.challenge: There are many landlocked countries and very few shortcuts that work across the whole set.
sub_saharan_africa.studyTip: Practice the regional sets first. This quiz works better as a combination test than as the place to learn every country from scratch.

americas.overview: The Americas round combines North America, Central America, the Caribbean and South America. The map swings between huge mainland countries and tiny islands.
americas.challenge: The scale changes constantly. Caribbean questions are especially easy to miss after a run of large countries.
americas.studyTip: Get North and South America comfortable on their own. Central America and the Caribbean are the bridge that makes the combined set harder.

eurasia.overview: Eurasia puts Europe and Asia on one continuous map. It is a huge set, from the Atlantic edge to the Pacific, with every kind of country size in between.
eurasia.challenge: A tiny European state and one of the world's largest countries can appear back to back. The constant scale change is the real difficulty.
eurasia.studyTip: Eurasia works better as a combination quiz after Europe and the Asian subregions already feel familiar.

former_soviet_union.overview: This group contains the countries that became independent after the Soviet Union dissolved. They stretch from the Baltics through the Caucasus and into Central Asia.
former_soviet_union.challenge: The five Central Asian countries are a common source of confusion, especially when the names are more familiar than the shapes.
former_soviet_union.studyTip: The Baltics, eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia are four useful chunks. Each has a different map pattern.

tiny_countries.overview: Tiny Countries collects small sovereign states from several parts of the world. Many of them are barely visible at normal world-map zoom.
tiny_countries.challenge: Screen size is the main problem. Some answers are so small that knowing the neighborhood matters more than recognizing an outline.
tiny_countries.studyTip: Group them by region. European microstates are one batch, and the island countries make more sense by ocean.

small_island_countries.overview: This set pulls small sovereign island countries from several oceans and regions. Most of them show up as tiny shapes or points on the world map.
small_island_countries.challenge: The answers are scattered far apart, so there is rarely a neat chain of land borders to follow.
small_island_countries.studyTip: Ocean and subregion groups make this set much less random than one giant list.

pacific_islands.overview: This set is the independent Pacific island countries in Smurdy's group list. Australia and New Zealand are left out so the smaller island states get the attention.
pacific_islands.challenge: The ocean distances are huge, and several countries are tiny on the map.
pacific_islands.studyTip: Papua New Guinea and Fiji are useful reference points. Once those are fixed, the rest is mostly an ocean-position problem.

find-country/asia.title: Asia Without Borders Quiz: Find All 51 Countries | Smurdy
find-country/asia.h1: Asia Without Borders Quiz: Find All 51 Countries
find-country/asia.metaDescription: Find all 51 countries of Asia without borders in this interactive blank-map quiz. Practice Asian geography using coastlines, islands, and relative position.
find-country/asia.lead: All the country borders are gone in this Asia quiz. You still have the coast, islands and peninsulas, so the job is figuring out where each name belongs from the shape of the continent itself.
find-country/asia.overviewHeading: Countries included in the Asia without-borders quiz
find-country/asia.overview: The full Asia set reaches from Turkey and Cyprus across Central and South Asia to Japan, Indonesia and Timor-Leste. With no internal lines, familiar subregions matter more than individual country outlines.
find-country/asia.howToPlay: A country name appears over a blank political map. Click roughly where it belongs and keep going through the set. The coastline stays visible.
find-country/asia.gameplayTip: If an inland country feels impossible, find the nearest sea, peninsula or country-sized shape you know first.
find-country/asia.challengeHeading: Hardest parts of a borderless Asia map
find-country/asia.challenge: Central Asia is the part most likely to turn into empty space. Mainland Southeast Asia is different: the countries are narrow and packed along a complicated coast.
find-country/asia.studyTip: Give each subregion one physical feature you can picture. The Caspian Sea is useful for Central Asia; India does the same job for South Asia.
find-country/asia.sectionBody: Trace the continent around Arabia, India and Southeast Asia before worrying about the inland countries. Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia and Sri Lanka also give the empty ocean some structure.

find-country/europe.title: Europe Without Borders Quiz: Find All 44 Countries | Smurdy
find-country/europe.h1: Europe Without Borders Quiz: Find All 44 Countries
find-country/europe.metaDescription: Find all 44 countries of Europe on a map without borders. Use coastlines, peninsulas, islands, and regional memory in this difficult Europe map quiz.
find-country/europe.lead: Europe gets much harder when the borders disappear. The coastlines and peninsulas are still there, but the small countries in the middle no longer have boxes around them.
find-country/europe.overview: All 44 European countries are in the round, including the microstates. Western Europe is fairly forgiving; Central Europe and the Balkans can be off by only a small distance.
find-country/europe.howToPlay: Smurdy names a country on a borderless Europe map. Click where it belongs. The outer coastline and islands stay visible for reference.
find-country/europe.gameplayTip: The big peninsulas are the easiest places to get your bearings when the middle of the map starts looking blank.
find-country/europe.challengeHeading: Why Europe is difficult without country borders
find-country/europe.challenge: Benelux, Central Europe and the Balkans leave very little room for a sloppy click once the outlines vanish.
find-country/europe.studyTip: Know Iberia, Italy and Scandinavia well. For the crowded parts, neighbor order is more useful than trying to imagine every missing border at once.
find-country/europe.sectionBody: Luxembourg, Kosovo, Montenegro and the microstates are unforgiving on a blank map. A rough idea of the region is not enough there.
find-country/europe.exampleSentence: Italy and Iberia are still obvious. Benelux and the western Balkans are where the map starts getting mean.

click-country/eurasia.title: Eurasia Map Quiz: Click All 95 Countries | Smurdy
click-country/eurasia.h1: Eurasia Map Quiz: Click All 95 Countries
click-country/eurasia.metaDescription: Learn the countries of Europe and Asia together in one 95-country Eurasia map quiz. Click each country using visible borders, shapes, and neighboring regions.
click-country/eurasia.lead: This is Europe and Asia in one long bordered-map round. The next question might be in Portugal, the Caucasus or the Pacific side of Asia.
click-country/eurasia.overviewHeading: What counts as Eurasia in this map quiz
click-country/eurasia.overview: The set joins the Europe and Asia groups on one continuous landmass. Questions can jump thousands of miles from one side of the map to the other.
click-country/eurasia.howToPlay: Read the country name and click the bordered shape. Keep going until the full Eurasia set is done.
click-country/eurasia.gameplayTip: Get the subregion right before you worry about the exact outline. That is usually faster than scanning the entire continent.
click-country/eurasia.challengeHeading: What makes the full Eurasia map difficult
click-country/eurasia.challenge: The scale is all over the place. Tiny European states can appear right beside enormous Asian countries in the same run.
click-country/eurasia.studyTip: Europe and the major Asian subregions should already feel familiar. Eurasia is best used for practicing the jumps between them.
click-country/eurasia.sectionBody: The Black Sea, Caucasus and Caspian area is the part worth learning carefully. It stops the middle of the map from feeling like a vague gap between Europe and Central Asia.

type-country/eurasia.title: Name All 95 Countries of Eurasia: Typing Quiz | Smurdy
type-country/eurasia.h1: Name All 95 Countries of Eurasia: Typing Quiz
type-country/eurasia.metaDescription: Name and type all 95 countries of Europe and Asia in this Eurasia map quiz. Practice country spelling, recognition, and location across one combined map.
type-country/eurasia.lead: This is the long version of the typing quiz: Europe and Asia on one map, with every highlighted country needing a name.
type-country/eurasia.overviewHeading: Countries covered by the Eurasia typing quiz
type-country/eurasia.overview: The round runs from Western Europe to East Asia. The difficulty is keeping a lot of country names ready at once.
type-country/eurasia.howToPlay: A country is highlighted on the bordered Eurasia map. Type the name and move on to the next one.
type-country/eurasia.gameplayTip: If you know the location but the name is slow, pause before typing. That tells you whether the problem is spelling or recall.
type-country/eurasia.challengeHeading: Recognition and spelling challenges in Eurasia
type-country/eurasia.challenge: Similar names and long multiword names slow this mode down even when the map itself is easy. The tiny states add a separate visual problem.
type-country/eurasia.studyTipHeading: Names that deserve their own practice
type-country/eurasia.studyTip: The Balkans, the -stan countries and the Caucasus are worth short spelling sessions. A few stubborn names do not need another full-map run.
type-country/eurasia.sectionBody: When you miss one, notice why. A country you recognized but could not name needs different practice from one you placed in the wrong part of the map.

find-country/south_america.title: South America Without Borders Quiz: Find 12 Countries | Smurdy
find-country/south_america.h1: South America Without Borders Quiz: Find 12 Countries
find-country/south_america.metaDescription: Find all 12 countries of South America on a blank map without borders. Use coastlines, Brazil, the Andes, and relative position in this geography quiz.
find-country/south_america.lead: South America only has 12 sovereign-country answers here, but removing the internal lines makes the north and the landlocked middle much less obvious.
find-country/south_america.overview: The round includes every sovereign country on the continent. Brazil fills most of the center and east; Bolivia and Paraguay are the two landlocked answers.
find-country/south_america.howToPlay: A country name appears on a South America map with the internal borders removed. Click its approximate location and keep going through all 12.
find-country/south_america.gameplayTip: Brazil touches most of the continent, so it is the easiest country to judge the others against.
find-country/south_america.challenge: Uruguay and Paraguay can blur together near southern Brazil. Colombia and Venezuela split the northern coast, and Guyana and Suriname are easy to reverse.
find-country/south_america.studyTip: The Pacific side has a clean north-to-south order. The two landlocked countries are also worth learning as a pair.
find-country/south_america.sectionHeading: Why French Guiana is not an answer
find-country/south_america.sectionBody: French Guiana appears on the northeastern coast between Suriname and Brazil, but it is an overseas department of France rather than a sovereign country. This quiz therefore includes Guyana and Suriname among its 12 answers, but not French Guiana.
find-country/south_america.exampleSentence: Chile is hard to lose. The northeast around Guyana and Suriname is where a blank map gets less friendly.

find-subdivision/us_states.title: US States Without Borders Quiz: Find All 50 States | Smurdy
find-subdivision/us_states.h1: US States Without Borders Quiz: Find All 50 States
find-subdivision/us_states.metaDescription: Find all 50 US states on a map without state borders. Practice American geography using coastlines, regions, and relative location in this difficult quiz.
find-subdivision/us_states.lead: The state lines are gone. You get the outline of the United States and have to place all 50 states from your mental map.
find-subdivision/us_states.overview: The quiz includes the 48 contiguous states plus Alaska and Hawaii. With the internal lines hidden, rectangle-shaped states stop being easy just because you recognize their outline.
find-subdivision/us_states.howToPlay: A state name appears on a US map with the state borders removed. Click where it belongs. Coastlines and the national outline stay visible.
find-subdivision/us_states.gameplayTip: Find the region first. A rough click from the whole national map is usually worse than narrowing it to the right part of the country.
find-subdivision/us_states.challengeHeading: Hardest US regions without state lines
find-subdivision/us_states.challenge: The Northeast is crowded, and the Great Plains lose the rectangular borders that normally do half the work for you.
find-subdivision/us_states.studyTip: The coasts and Great Lakes give you useful structure. The Plains and interior West need more pure position memory.
find-subdivision/us_states.sectionHeading: Why Washington, DC is not included
find-subdivision/us_states.sectionBody: Washington, DC is a federal district, so it is not one of the 50 state answers in this quiz.
find-subdivision/us_states.exampleSentence: Florida and Michigan still give you obvious shapes. Kansas does not.

click-country/europe.title: Europe Map Quiz: Click All 44 Countries | Smurdy
click-country/europe.h1: Europe Map Quiz: Click All 44 Countries
click-country/europe.metaDescription: Learn all 44 countries of Europe with an interactive click map quiz. Use visible borders, shapes, coastlines, and neighbors to practice European geography.
click-country/europe.lead: This is the standard Europe map quiz: a country name appears, the borders stay visible and you click the matching shape.
click-country/europe.overview: All 44 countries are here, from the big peninsulas and islands to the microstates. Most players get slowed down in the crowded middle of the continent.
click-country/europe.howToPlay: Read the country name and click its bordered area. A wrong click stays useful because you can see exactly which neighbor you chose.
click-country/europe.gameplayTip: When two small countries keep swapping places, learn the border they share rather than memorizing both shapes separately.
click-country/europe.challenge: The Balkans, Central Europe, and the Benelux region place many countries close together, while microstates can be difficult to select at normal zoom. Similar-looking Baltic and Balkan locations also reward careful neighbor checking.
click-country/europe.studyTip: Begin with distinctive outer shapes such as Portugal, Italy, Greece, Norway, and the United Kingdom. Add Central Europe, the Baltics, and the Balkans as separate clusters, then combine them in the full 44-country quiz.
click-country/europe.sectionBody: Visible borders make this quiz ideal for learning which countries touch. Notice Portugal west of Spain, the Baltic states in north-to-south order, the countries surrounding Germany, and the chain running down the western Balkans. Those relationships remain useful in harder modes.
click-country/europe.exampleSentence: France, Italy, and Spain make useful reference points before you get into places such as Andorra, Slovenia, or North Macedonia.

click-country/south_america.title: South America Map Quiz: Click All 12 Countries | Smurdy
click-country/south_america.h1: South America Map Quiz: Click All 12 Countries
click-country/south_america.metaDescription: Learn all 12 countries of South America with an interactive map quiz. Click each visible country outline and practice borders, neighbors, and locations.
click-country/south_america.lead: Learn the 12 sovereign countries of South America by clicking their visible map outlines. The compact set is ideal for practicing country shapes, shared borders, coastlines, and regional order.
click-country/south_america.overview: This quiz covers all 12 sovereign South American countries. The map runs from Colombia, Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname in the north through Brazil and the inland states to Chile, Argentina, and Uruguay in the south.
click-country/south_america.howToPlay: Read the country name, find its bordered shape on the South America map, and click it. Continue through all 12 answers, using coastlines and neighboring countries whenever a shape is unfamiliar.
click-country/south_america.gameplayTip: Locate Brazil first as the continent's biggest reference point, then compare the target with the countries around its border.
click-country/south_america.challengeHeading: South American countries commonly mixed up
click-country/south_america.challenge: Guyana and Suriname are small neighbors on the northeastern coast, while Uruguay and Paraguay are sometimes confused because both sit near southern Brazil. Bolivia's inland position can also be mistaken for neighboring Peru or Paraguay.
click-country/south_america.studyTipHeading: The fastest way to learn the South America map
click-country/south_america.studyTip: Memorize the Pacific coast from Colombia to Chile, then learn the northern Atlantic countries and the Southern Cone. Add Bolivia and Paraguay last as the two landlocked countries, always relating them back to Brazil.
click-country/south_america.sectionHeading: Use Brazil to organize the continent
click-country/south_america.sectionBody: Brazil borders every sovereign South American country except Chile and Ecuador. That makes one question especially useful: does the target touch Brazil? Combining that fact with the Pacific and Atlantic coastlines quickly narrows most answers.
click-country/south_america.exampleSentence: Brazil is the obvious reference point, while Chile, Uruguay, Paraguay, and the Guianas force you to read the edges more carefully.

type-capital/us_states.title: Type the US State Capitals Quiz | Smurdy
type-capital/us_states.h1: Type the US State Capitals Quiz
type-capital/us_states.metaDescription: Practice all 50 US state capitals on an interactive map. Each state is highlighted, you type its capital, and the capital city is briefly marked after every answer.
type-capital/us_states.lead: Learn all 50 US state capitals with the same state map used by Smurdy's other US geography quizzes.
type-capital/us_states.overviewHeading: What the US state capitals quiz covers
type-capital/us_states.overview: This quiz includes all 50 states and their current capital cities. Each question keeps the state visible on the map so you learn the capital together with its geographic location.
type-capital/us_states.challenge: Many state capitals are not the state's largest or best-known city. Pairs such as New York and Albany, California and Sacramento, and Nevada and Carson City reward direct recall instead of guessing the most famous city.
type-capital/us_states.studyTipHeading: How to learn the 50 state capitals
type-capital/us_states.studyTip: Learn capitals by region first, then mix the full set. The Northeast and Midwest are useful clusters because several states and capitals are packed closely together.
type-capital/us_states.sectionHeading: Why Washington, DC is not included
type-capital/us_states.sectionBody: Washington, DC is the capital of the United States, not a state capital. This quiz covers exactly the 50 states, so the answer set contains 50 state capitals.
type-capital/us_states.exampleSentence: Albany, Sacramento, Carson City, Juneau, and Austin are all in the same 50-answer set.

click-country/world.exampleSentence: One round can jump from Argentina to Kyrgyzstan to Fiji with no warning.

click-country/africa.exampleSentence: Nigeria, Ethiopia, South Africa, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo are good large reference points for filling in the harder neighbors.

click-country/spanish_speaking.exampleSentence: Mexico, Spain, and Equatorial Guinea make the geographic spread of the set pretty obvious.

type-country/asia.exampleSentence: Kazakhstan, Thailand, the Philippines, and the smaller Central Asian countries test very different kinds of recall.

type-country/tiny_countries.exampleSentence: Monaco, San Marino, Liechtenstein, Tuvalu, and Nauru are small enough that location context matters as much as outline shape.
type-country/tiny_countries.sectionHeading: Typing tiny places is its own problem
type-country/tiny_countries.sectionBody: A country can be visually obvious once you notice it and still be hard to name quickly. This set is good at separating those two skills.

find-country/africa.exampleSentence: The Mediterranean coast, the Horn, Madagascar, and South Africa are useful reference points before you work inland.

find-point/world.exampleSentence: A point in Canada is one thing; a point near the edge of Rwanda, Belgium, or El Salvador is another.

find-point/europe.sectionBody: Europe makes this mode noticeably harder because a small movement can cross several national borders in a compact part of the map.

type-capital/world.exampleSentence: A round can move from Ottawa to Abuja, then Bishkek, Suva, and Montevideo.

type-capital/africa.exampleSentence: Nairobi and Addis Ababa are familiar starting points; Brazzaville and Kinshasa are a pair worth learning together.
type-capital/africa.sectionBody: The two Congos are especially easy to reverse, and several countries have capitals that are less famous than another city in the same country.

type-capital/europe.exampleSentence: Madrid and Rome usually come quickly; Ljubljana, Bratislava, Podgorica, and Chisinau are better tests of full recall.

type-capital/spanish_speaking.exampleSentence: The set runs from Mexico City and Santo Domingo to Madrid and Malabo.

type-capital/caribbean_islands.exampleSentence: Havana, Santo Domingo, Kingston, Nassau, and Bridgetown all appear here.

click-subdivision/us_states.exampleSentence: California and Texas are easy reference points; the Northeast and the cluster around Missouri demand much closer reading.

type-subdivision/us_states.exampleSentence: You may recognize Oklahoma, West Virginia, or Connecticut instantly and still need an extra second to pull the name out.

find-point-subdivision/us_states.overviewHeading: How well do you know state boundaries?
find-point-subdivision/us_states.exampleSentence: A point near New York City, Kansas City, or the Four Corners can punish a rough mental map very quickly.
